name: Stylo (Rust parallel CSS style engine in Firefox Quantum) vs Gecko's previous C++ style system
baseline: Gecko's previous sequential C++ style system (CSS selector matching and cascade) in Firefox before Quantum
workload: Firefox page load of Amazon's homepage, where style computation runs as a parallel work-stealing top-down cascade (rayon) instead of the old single-threaded C++ cascade.
claimed_speedup: 30% page load speedup for Amazon's homepage ('Parallelism leads to a lot of performance improvements, including a 30% page load speedup for Amazon's homepage'). Stylo replaces about 160,000 lines of C++ with 85,000 lines of Rust.
stars_or_usage: 340 stars (servo/stylo); ships in Firefox since Quantum (version 57) and in Servo
tradeoffs: Not a standalone library: it is wired into Gecko or Servo through Rust-to-C++ FFI and a DOM abstraction, and it needs those hosts to call back into C++ for some data. The blog says occasional calls into C++ code off the main thread surfaced thread-safety bugs in the C++ side (caches, global mutable state). Parallelism helps large pages and many cores; tiny documents gain little.
caveats: First-party blog (Rust blog post by a Servo/Mozilla engineer, 2017-11-14) with a single headline number: no workload details beyond 'Amazon's homepage', no hardware, core count, Firefox build flags, run count or comparison builds, and no benchmark code. The comparison is Firefox with Stylo against Firefox with the old C++ style system, so it mixes the rewrite's other optimizations with the parallelism; a Mozilla Hacks post (hacks.mozilla.org was blocked here, so seen only as a WebSearch snippet) says the engine borrows optimizations from other browsers and would be fast without parallelism, and gives a best-case 'up to 2, 4 or even 18 times faster' style-computation range that scales with core count (snippet only, not verified). Baseline is a production C++ build, probably with PGO and LTO, but this is not stated. The repo servo/stylo is Servo's downstream copy of the code that lives in mozilla-central (the Firefox repo, already on the known list); it carries no benchmark. The blog's 'two earlier C++ attempts to parallelize the style system failed' is a claim about engineering difficulty, not a measurement.
found_via: WebSearch 'Stylo Quantum CSS Rust parallel style system faster than Gecko C++ style system speedup cores hacks.mozilla.org' surfaced the Rust blog and Hacks posts; the Rust blog source was opened on raw.githubusercontent.com (rust-lang/blog.rust-lang.org) and servo/stylo on github.com.
why_faster: Rust's ownership and Send/Sync checking made it practical to run the top-down style cascade in parallel with a rayon work-stealing traversal (child styles are independent once the parent is computed), where two earlier C++ attempts failed on thread-safety bugs. Stylo also shares computed style structs through Arc. The Hacks post additionally credits optimizations borrowed from other browsers (snippet only).

name: Erlang/OTP processes on thread-ring (SCOOP/Qs paper, arXiv 1405.7153) vs C++/TBB
baseline: C++ with Intel TBB (the paper authors' own implementation) on the thread-ring benchmark; a pthread or std::thread ring is not what the paper table is reported to use
workload: thread-ring: 503 threads or processes arranged in a ring pass a token a fixed number of times; the paper (per the search snippet) calls it essentially single-threaded and a test of context-switching overhead. Timed on a 32-core machine.
claimed_speedup: Thread-ring on 32 cores (snippet only): Erlang 3.30 s versus C++/TBB 34.13 s, about 10x (derived from the snippet numbers).
tradeoffs: BEAM gives cheap processes and preemptive per-process scheduling with garbage-collected per-process heaps; a language runtime is required, and raw single-thread compute is slower than C++. Calling C needs NIFs or ports.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from two independent WebSearch result summaries of the 2014 arXiv paper 'Efficient and Reasonable Object-Oriented Concurrency' (arXiv 1405.7153, SCOOP/Qs authors); arxiv.org is blocked in this environment, so the paper, its benchmark code, compiler versions and flags, and the exact C++ implementation were not opened (benchmark_url is null for that reason). The C++ baseline is reported as C++/TBB, whose task scheduler is not designed for a ring of 503 blocking threads, so a hand-written futex or fiber ring in C++ would likely be far faster: the Boost.Fiber documentation (opened by a sibling search) shows C++ fibers matching or beating Go and Erlang on skynet. In the same snippet table Haskell was slower (57.44 s) and SCOOP/Qs took 5.82 s. Toolchains date from about 2014. Treat as a lead for a paper-access retier, not as a confirmed win.
found_via: WebSearch 'thread-ring benchmark Erlang OR Haskell OR Go faster than C++ pthreads lightweight threads blog results seconds' returned arxiv.org/pdf/1405.7153 (summary of its table); the repo page was opened on github.com for license, stars and last commit.
why_faster: Inferred, not argued by the snippet: Erlang processes are lightweight units switched by the BEAM scheduler in user space, and the benchmark is context-switch bound, so the cost per switch dominates.

name: Go goroutines on thread-ring (SCOOP/Qs paper, arXiv 1405.7153) vs C++/TBB
baseline: C++ with Intel TBB (the paper authors' own implementation) on the thread-ring benchmark; a pthread or std::thread ring is not what the paper table is reported to use
workload: thread-ring: 503 threads or processes arranged in a ring pass a token a fixed number of times; the paper (per the search snippet) calls it essentially single-threaded and a test of context-switching overhead. Timed on a 32-core machine.
claimed_speedup: Thread-ring on 32 cores (snippet only): Go 13.98 s versus C++/TBB 34.13 s, about 2.4x (derived from the snippet numbers); Erlang took 3.30 s in the same table.
tradeoffs: Go gives cheap goroutines and channels but adds a garbage-collected runtime, a fixed scheduler policy and slower cgo calls into C; stacks grow dynamically.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from two independent WebSearch result summaries of the 2014 arXiv paper 'Efficient and Reasonable Object-Oriented Concurrency' (arXiv 1405.7153, SCOOP/Qs authors); arxiv.org is blocked in this environment, so the paper, its benchmark code, compiler versions and flags, and the exact C++ implementation were not opened (benchmark_url is null for that reason). The C++ baseline is reported as C++/TBB, whose task scheduler is not designed for a ring of 503 blocking threads, so a hand-written futex or fiber ring in C++ would likely be far faster: the Boost.Fiber documentation (opened by a sibling search) shows C++ fibers matching or beating Go and Erlang on skynet. In the same snippet table Haskell was slower (57.44 s) and SCOOP/Qs took 5.82 s. Toolchains date from about 2014. Treat as a lead for a paper-access retier, not as a confirmed win.
found_via: WebSearch 'thread-ring benchmark Erlang OR Haskell OR Go faster than C++ pthreads lightweight threads blog results seconds' returned arxiv.org/pdf/1405.7153 (summary of its table); the repo page was opened on github.com for license, stars and last commit.
why_faster: Inferred, not argued by the snippet: goroutines are user-space units multiplexed by the Go scheduler onto OS threads and a channel hand-off is cheaper than an OS-thread wake-up. Go's own 13.98 s is 4x slower than Erlang in the same table, so the ranking is scheduler-specific.
